cloze.text: Diuretics lower blood pressure by preventing {{c1::sodium}} reabsorption in the kidneys, especially in the {{c2::Loop of Henle}} and {{c2::distal tubule}}.
cloze.extra: Water follows sodium — more sodium out means more water out.

cloze.text: Bradykinin is a natural chemical that causes blood vessels to {{c1::dilate}}; when it builds up (as with ACE inhibitors) it can trigger coughing and, rarely, swelling called {{c2::angioedema}}.
{{c1::Calcium channel blockers}} can cause gingival hyperplasia, especially {{c2::nifedipine}}; the overgrowth is not caused by plaque but {{c3::worsens with poor oral hygiene}}.
cloze.extra: They alter how cells in the gingiva grow.

cloze.text: Beta blockers are no longer considered {{c1::first-line}} for basic hypertension, but remain essential when the patient also has previous MI, angina, {{c2::arrhythmias}} or anxiety.
Anti-anginal agents treat {{c1::angina pectoris}} — chest pain due to {{c2::reduced oxygen to the heart muscle}}.
Anti-anginal agents work by {{c1::dilating blood vessels}} (especially the coronary arteries) to improve oxygen supply and reduce heart workload.
Anti-anginal generic drugs: {{c1::nitroglycerin}}, isosorbide dinitrate and isosorbide mononitrate; brand names include {{c2::Nitrostat}} and Nitro-Dur.
Heart failure agents treat {{c1::congestive heart failure}} (weakened pumping, fluid overload).
Heart failure agents: {{c1::digoxin}} increases the force of heart contractions; {{c2::spironolactone}} blocks aldosterone, reducing fluid retention.
Brand names of heart failure agents: {{c1::Lanoxin}} = digoxin; {{c2::Aldactone}} = spironolactone.
Anti-arrhythmia agents treat irregular heart rhythms such as {{c1::atrial fibrillation}}, tachycardia ({{c2::fast}}) and bradycardia ({{c3::slow}}).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Tachycardia (fast) → think "taxi is fast". Bradycardia (slow) → braiding hair is a slow process!

cloze.text: Anti-arrhythmia agents' mechanism varies by class: they block {{c1::sodium, potassium or calcium}} channels, or block {{c2::sympathetic input}} (beta blockers).
Anti-arrhythmia generic drugs include disopyramide, quinidine, mexiletine, atenolol, {{c1::metoprolol}}, {{c2::amiodarone}}, diltiazem, verapamil and {{c3::lidocaine}}.
Anti-arrhythmia brand names: {{c1::Lopressor}} (metoprolol), {{c2::Cardizem}} (diltiazem), {{c3::Isoptin}} (verapamil), {{c4::Xylocaine}} (lidocaine).
cloze.extra: The book also lists Rhythmodan (disopyramide), Inderal and Multaq. Note: Inderal is propranolol and Multaq is dronedarone — neither is in the book's generic list.

cloze.text: Anticoagulants/antiplatelets are used for {{c1::prevention of clots}} (stroke, MI, valve replacement, stents).
{{c1::Warfarin}} inhibits {{c2::vitamin K}}-dependent clotting factors; aspirin and clopidogrel inhibit {{c3::platelets}}.
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet brand names: {{c1::Coumadin}} (warfarin), Bayer Aspirin, {{c2::Plavix}} (clopidogrel).
Antihyperlipidemic agents (statins) treat {{c1::high cholesterol}} (especially {{c2::LDL}}) and prevent {{c3::atherosclerosis}}.
Statins inhibit the {{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}} enzyme to reduce {{c2::liver}} cholesterol production.
Side effects of anti-anginal agents: headache, flushing, dizziness and {{c1::hypotension}}.
Side effects of heart failure agents: increased salivation and gag reflex ({{c1::digoxin}}); {{c2::hyperkalemia}} (spironolactone).
Side effects of anti-arrhythmia agents: {{c1::bradycardia}}, AV block, dizziness, and possible {{c2::gingival hyperplasia}} (with calcium channel blockers).
Side effects of anticoagulants/antiplatelets: excessive {{c1::bleeding}}, bruising, hemorrhage.
Side effects of statins: muscle pain ({{c1::myalgia}}), {{c2::liver enzyme}} elevation, possible GI upset.
Dental relevance of anti-anginal agents: raise the chair {{c1::slowly}} (risk of hypotension); nitroglycerin is provided {{c2::sublingually}}.
Dental relevance of heart failure agents: avoid {{c1::high-dose epinephrine}} because {{c2::digoxin}} increases risk of arrhythmia; watch for excessive gag reflex.
Dental relevance of anti-arrhythmia agents: monitor vitals; avoid high epinephrine with {{c1::beta blockers}}; confirm {{c2::pacemaker}} presence if applicable.
Dental relevance of warfarin: ensure INR ≤ {{c1::3}} before invasive treatment; avoid {{c2::NSAIDs}} and use {{c3::acetaminophen}} for pain.
Statins have {{c1::no direct oral effects}}, but the patient should report {{c2::muscle pain}} if present.
Nitrates: {{c1::tolerance}} develops with regular use; do not mix with {{c2::erectile dysfunction}} meds.
Besides heart failure, spironolactone is also used to treat {{c1::liver}}-related fluid retention.
The anti-arrhythmic drug class is selected based on arrhythmia type (e.g., {{c1::atrial vs. ventricular}}); it may be used short- or long-term.
{{c1::Baby aspirin (81 mg)}} is often used for clot prevention and is usually safe for dental patients.
Statins reduce cardiovascular events by lowering LDL and {{c1::stabilizing arterial plaques}}.
Cardiovascular drugs support the heart and blood vessels by improving circulation, heart function, oxygen delivery, {{c1::rhythm control}} and blood flow.

Cardiovascular drugs differ from antihypertensives: they treat chest pain, heart failure, arrhythmias, clot risk and high cholesterol, while antihypertensives are used specifically to {{c1::lower blood pressure}}.
Some drugs — like {{c1::beta blockers}} and {{c1::calcium channel blockers}} — are used in both cardiovascular therapy and antihypertensive treatment.
{{c1::Prothrombin time (PT)}} measures how long it takes blood to clot and is used to monitor {{c2::warfarin}} (Coumadin).
{{c1::Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)}} is another test of clotting ability; normal range {{c2::25–35}} seconds.
The {{c1::INR (International Normalized Ratio)}} compares the patient's clotting time to normal; an INR of about {{c2::1.0}} is normal for healthy people.
INR > {{c1::3.0}} = consult the physician before invasive procedures; INR ≥ {{c2::3.5}} = high risk of prolonged bleeding.
NSAIDs treat pain, {{c1::inflammation}} and fever (e.g., post-op dental swelling, arthritis, injury).
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) treats pain and fever — but {{c1::not inflammation}}.
Opioids treat {{c1::moderate to severe}} pain and provide sedation (e.g., surgery, extraction, trauma).
NSAIDs work by blocking the enzymes {{c1::COX-1}} and {{c1::COX-2}}, which trigger swelling and pain.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "NSAIDs = No Sticky AID for clots" → they stop platelets from sticking, so NSAIDs inhibit clotting and increase bleeding risk.

cloze.text: Acetaminophen works in the {{c1::brain}} to reduce pain and lower body temperature.
Opioids bind to pain receptors in the brain and spinal cord ({{c1::mu}}, kappa, delta) to block pain; they are {{c2::depressants}}.
Opioid-group drugs listed include codeine, morphine, oxycodone, hydrocodone, fentanyl, methadone and the opioid reversal agent {{c1::naloxone}}.
NSAID brand names: {{c1::Advil}} and {{c1::Motrin}} = ibuprofen; {{c2::Aleve}} = naproxen; Bayer = aspirin.
Side effects of NSAIDs: stomach upset, {{c1::ulcers}}, kidney issues, {{c2::bleeding risk}} (especially aspirin long-term).
Acetaminophen can cause {{c1::liver damage}} if too much is taken or it is mixed with {{c2::alcohol}}.
Opioid side effects: drowsiness, {{c1::constipation}}, pinpoint pupils ({{c2::miosis}}), addiction, slowed breathing.
Do NOT use NSAIDs if the patient has {{c1::ulcers}}, kidney problems, or is taking {{c2::blood thinners}} (e.g., warfarin).
Do NOT use acetaminophen if the patient has {{c1::liver disease}} or drinks alcohol regularly.
Do NOT use opioids if the patient has {{c1::breathing problems}}, an addiction history, or is already overly sedated.
Dental relevance of NSAIDs: avoid in {{c1::bleeding-risk}} patients; they help reduce swelling and pain after procedures.
{{c1::Acetaminophen}} is the preferred pain reliever for patients with ulcers, kidney issues, or on warfarin.
{{c1::Codeine}} is the opioid common in dentistry; watch for sedation or abuse risk.
NSAIDs work best when taken {{c1::before pain worsens}}; do not mix multiple NSAIDs.
Acetaminophen is included in many combo meds — {{c1::double dosing}} risk; stick to a maximum of {{c2::3000–4000 mg/day}}.
{{c1::Naloxone (Narcan)}} reverses opioid overdose; overdose signs = coma, {{c2::slowed breathing}}, {{c3::pinpoint pupils}}.
cloze.extra: Did you know? In 2022 there were over 109,000 drug overdose deaths in the US, ~75% involving opioids (CDC).

cloze.text: NSAIDs block {{c1::COX-1}} (found all over the body — especially stomach, kidneys and platelets) and {{c2::COX-2}} (found mainly in injured or inflamed tissues).
cloze.extra: This is why NSAIDs help inflammation but can upset the stomach or hurt the kidneys if overused.

cloze.text: NSAIDs are first-line treatment for {{c1::osteoarthritis}} and {{c1::rheumatoid arthritis}} because they reduce joint inflammation.
Of the NSAIDs, {{c1::aspirin}} especially interferes with clotting because it blocks the action of {{c2::platelets}}.
cloze.extra: NSAIDs are therefore contraindicated with warfarin (Coumadin); acetaminophen is the safer alternative.

cloze.text: Tylenol #3 (acetaminophen + codeine) gives more relief than acetaminophen alone and is common after {{c1::extractions}} or surgery; the codeine adds {{c2::sedation}} and constipation risk.
Narcan kicks opioids off the brain's receptors and works within {{c1::minutes}}; in emergencies EMS or trained staff use it to reverse coma and slow breathing.
Oxycodone is a {{c1::semi-synthetic}} opioid — chemically modified from natural opiates to enhance pain relief.
cloze.extra: Oxycodone combos (Percocet, Percodan) give stronger relief after dental surgery or severe pain but carry risks of sedation, constipation and addiction.

cloze.text: Opiate drugs come from the {{c1::opium poppy}} (Papaver somniferum).
Nitrous oxide is used to alleviate {{c1::anxiety}}; it can also relax {{c2::skeletal muscles}}, as in a patient with cerebral palsy.
Nitrous oxide provides stage {{c1::1}} anesthesia; the patient can {{c2::hear and respond}} to requests from the dentist.
cloze.extra: Stage 1 is the lowest, stage 4 the highest level of anesthesia.

cloze.text: Nitrous oxide undergoes {{c1::no biotransformation}} in the body; it is excreted through {{c2::exhalation}} and wears off soon after the mask is removed.
Once nitrous oxide flow is terminated, 100% oxygen should be delivered for {{c1::5}} minutes.
Nitrous oxide is contraindicated with respiratory issues such as {{c1::COPD}} or airway congestion, {{c2::pregnancy}}, cystic fibrosis, infections, depression, and history of {{c3::substance abuse}}.
cloze.extra: Obstructions reduce the amount of gas reaching the lungs and brain.

cloze.text: Gas tank colors: nitrous oxide = {{c1::blue}}; oxygen = {{c2::green}}.
Amoxicillin belongs to the {{c1::penicillin}} class and is {{c2::bactericidal}}.
Amoxicillin brand names: {{c1::Amoxil}}, Trimox.
Amoxicillin is the {{c1::first-line}} antibiotic for premedication.
cloze.extra: Dental hygiene tip: confirm penicillin allergy first. AHA 2021 (exam standard) prophylaxis: amoxicillin 2 g adult / 50 mg/kg child, single oral dose 30–60 min before the procedure.

cloze.text: Common dental uses of amoxicillin: premedication, {{c1::abscess}}, cellulitis; it covers {{c2::gram-positive}} and some gram-negative bacteria.
Prophylactic amoxicillin dose: {{c1::2 g}} for adults, {{c2::50 mg/kg}} for children, before the appointment.
cloze.extra: Book: "1 hr before appt"; AHA 2021 (exam standard): single dose 30–60 minutes before the procedure.

cloze.text: Amoxicillin treatment dosing for adults: 500 mg every {{c1::8}} hours (q8h).
Amoxicillin strengths: {{c1::broad-spectrum}}, well absorbed. Side effects: GI upset, rash, {{c2::cross-allergy}}. Pregnancy: {{c3::safe}}.
Azithromycin is a {{c1::macrolide}} and is {{c2::bacteriostatic}}.
Azithromycin brand names: {{c1::Zithromax}}, {{c1::Z-Pak}}.
Azithromycin is used for premedication in patients with {{c1::penicillin allergy}}; it targets {{c2::intracellular}} bacteria.
cloze.extra: AHA 2021 (exam standard) prophylaxis dose: 500 mg adult / 15 mg/kg child, single dose 30–60 min before. The book's tip "use if clindamycin not tolerated" is outdated — clindamycin is no longer recommended for prophylaxis (AHA 2021).

cloze.text: Azithromycin treatment dosing: adults {{c1::500 mg day 1, then 250 mg × 4}} days; children 10 mg/kg day 1, then 5 mg/kg.
cloze.extra: This is the treatment (Z-Pak) course, not the prophylaxis dose.

cloze.text: Azithromycin strength: {{c1::long half-life}}, convenient. Side effects: GI upset, {{c2::metallic taste}} (rare). Pregnancy: use with caution.
Penicillin VK is a {{c1::natural penicillin}} (β-lactam), bactericidal, brand Pen-VK; it is {{c2::not}} used for premedication.
Penicillin VK is used for {{c1::mild/moderate oral infections}} and covers mostly {{c2::gram-positive}} bacteria.
Penicillin VK dosing: adults 500 mg {{c1::q6h}} for 7–10 days; children 25–50 mg/kg/day divided.
cloze.extra: Effective but frequent dosing. Side effects: GI upset, rash, allergy. Pregnancy: safe.

cloze.text: Metronidazole is a {{c1::nitroimidazole}}, bactericidal; brand name {{c2::Flagyl}}; not used for premedication.
Metronidazole targets {{c1::anaerobic}} periodontal pathogens only (e.g., {{c2::P. gingivalis}}).
Metronidazole is very effective combined with {{c1::amoxicillin}}.
cloze.extra: Dosing: adults 250–500 mg q8–12h × 7–10 days; children: use with caution.

cloze.text: Metronidazole side effects: {{c1::metallic taste}}, black hairy tongue, and a reaction with {{c2::alcohol}}.
cloze.extra: Do not combine with alcohol. Pregnancy: avoid in the 1st trimester.

cloze.text: Cephalexin is a {{c1::cephalosporin}} (β-lactam), bactericidal; brand name {{c2::Keflex}}.
Cephalexin may be used for premedication only if the patient has {{c1::no history of anaphylaxis}} to penicillin, because it is structurally like penicillin ({{c2::cross-reactivity}}).
cloze.extra: Book: "yes — joint replacements if not anaphylactic". AHA 2021 (exam standard): cephalexin 2 g adult / 50 mg/kg child is an option for penicillin-allergic patients with NO history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.

cloze.text: Cephalexin covers {{c1::gram-positive cocci}}; dental uses: premed for prosthetic joints, mild infections.
cloze.extra: Dosing per the book: 2 g 1 hr before appt (child 50 mg/kg); treatment 500 mg q6h. Side effects: GI upset, rash, cross-reactivity with penicillins. Pregnancy: safe.

cloze.text: Side effects of anti-bacterial drugs include {{c1::superinfection}} and GI upset; e.g., {{c2::candidiasis}} (fungal) may follow antibiotic use.
{{c1::NSPT}} is the "gold" standard for reducing inflammation and gaining clinical attachment; antimicrobials are {{c2::adjunct}} therapy.
{{c1::Azithromycin}} is the main macrolide studied in dentistry as second-line premedication for penicillin-allergic patients; erythromycin and clarithromycin are less emphasized.
Systemic doxycycline brand names: {{c1::Vibramycin}}, Doryx.
Systemic doxycycline: oral capsule/tablet, {{c1::100 mg BID}}, daily dosing.
{{c1::Arestin}} = minocycline {{c2::1 mg microspheres}}, placed by syringe into pockets ≥ 5 mm (1 mg per pocket).
Arestin (minocycline) gives sustained release for up to {{c1::14}} days; the patient should not brush/floss the site for {{c2::7–10}} days.
{{c1::Atridox}} = {{c2::10% doxycycline hyclate gel}}, injected via cannula into pockets ≥ 5 mm (one dose per pocket, blunt-end syringe).
Atridox gives sustained release for {{c1::7}} days; avoid disturbing the area for 7 days.
{{c1::Periostat}} is a low-dose doxycycline oral capsule — systemic, {{c2::subantimicrobial}} dosing.
Periostat dosing: {{c1::20 mg}} twice daily, long-term use up to {{c2::9}} months.
Tetracyclines are {{c1::bacteriostatic}} and are used in dentistry to treat {{c2::periodontitis}}.
cloze.extra: They also cause photosensitivity — patients sunburn more easily.

cloze.text: Tetracycline tooth discoloration occurs when taken during permanent-teeth development — from the {{c1::second trimester}} of pregnancy up to about age {{c2::8 or 9}}.
Tetracycline deposits in the dentin and enamel cause permanent yellow, brown or grey discoloration that may {{c1::fluoresce}} under {{c2::UV light}}.
Tetracyclines cross the {{c1::placenta}} and interfere with fetal tooth and bone development, so they are contraindicated in pregnancy and {{c2::breastfeeding}}.
Patients taking tetracyclines may experience {{c1::photosensitivity}} — more likely to sunburn.
Chlorhexidine rinse is {{c1::0.12%}}, swished for {{c2::30 seconds}} twice daily.
Chlorhexidine rinse: duration of effect is {{c1::immediate and short-lived}} (rinse & spit); indications include post-SRP rinse, mucositis and {{c2::peri-implantitis}}.
Chlorhexidine rinse side effects: {{c1::staining}} of teeth and tongue, and {{c2::bitter or metallic}} taste alteration.
PerioChip is a {{c1::2.5 mg}} chlorhexidine gelatin chip inserted into pockets, with sustained release up to {{c2::10}} days.
PerioChip indications: {{c1::localized periodontitis}}, post-SRP adjunct; it causes {{c2::no}} staining or taste alteration.
cloze.extra: Dental tip: avoid disturbing the area for 7 days.

cloze.text: Chlorhexidine is a broad-spectrum {{c1::antiseptic}}, not an antibiotic; it works by disrupting bacterial {{c2::cell membranes}}, causing leakage and cell death.

basic.front: Why can ACE inhibitors cause a dry, persistent cough?
basic.back: They block the enzyme that breaks down bradykinin, so bradykinin builds up and irritates the lungs.

basic.front: Why are ARBs often used when a patient can't tolerate an ACE inhibitor?
basic.back: ARBs do not increase bradykinin, so they lower blood pressure like ACE inhibitors but without causing a cough.
It doesn't block COX-2 in the body like NSAIDs do; it mainly works in the brain, so it lowers pain and fever but doesn't help swelling/inflammation.
basic.extra: WakeUpMemory: acetamiNOphen → NO use for inflammation, NO effect on coagulation.

basic.front: Why is clindamycin no longer recommended for antibiotic premedication (ADA/AHA)?
basic.back: High risk of C. difficile colitis, increased mortality compared with amoxicillin, and limited benefit in preventing infective endocarditis.
A secondary infection superimposed on an earlier one, especially by a different microbe resistant to the treatment used against the first infection

mcq.question: A patient taking digoxin for congestive heart failure presents for scaling. Which precaution is most important?
options: A. Raise the chair slowly to prevent hypotension
B. Avoid high-dose epinephrine in local anesthetic
D. Avoid acetaminophen for post-op pain
mcq.answer: B. Avoid high-dose epinephrine in local anesthetic
mcq.explanation: Digoxin increases the risk of arrhythmia, so high-dose epinephrine is avoided (also watch for an excessive gag reflex). Raising the chair slowly is the precaution for anti-anginal agents (hypotension); INR applies to warfarin.

mcq.question: Which side effect is associated with spironolactone?
mcq.explanation: Spironolactone (Aldactone) can cause hyperkalemia. Increased salivation/gag reflex is digoxin; gingival hyperplasia is calcium channel blockers; myalgia is statins.

mcq.question: A patient on warfarin reports an INR of 3.4 this morning. Periodontal debridement is planned. What is the best action?
options: A. Proceed; this is the normal therapeutic target
B. Proceed, but prescribe an NSAID for post-op pain
C. Consult the physician before the invasive procedure
D. Order a PTT, since INR does not apply to warfarin
mcq.answer: C. Consult the physician before the invasive procedure
mcq.explanation: INR 2.0–3.0 is the usual warfarin target; INR > 3.0 = consult the physician before invasive treatment (≥ 3.5 = high risk of prolonged bleeding). NSAIDs are avoided with warfarin; PT/INR (not PTT) monitors warfarin.

mcq.question: A patient taking warfarin needs an analgesic after an extraction. Which is the best choice?
mcq.explanation: Acetaminophen has no anti-platelet effect and is preferred for patients on warfarin, with ulcers or kidney issues. Ibuprofen, naproxen and aspirin are NSAIDs that increase bleeding risk.

mcq.question: A patient who took an opioid is unresponsive with slowed breathing. Which pupil finding and drug are expected?
mcq.explanation: Opioid overdose = coma, slowed breathing, pinpoint pupils (miosis); naloxone (Narcan) reverses it.

mcq.question: For which patient is nitrous oxide–oxygen sedation contraindicated?
options: A. An anxious adult with controlled hypertension
B. A patient with cerebral palsy
D. A child with dental fear
mcq.explanation: COPD/airway obstruction reduces the gas reaching the lungs and brain. N₂O can actually help relax skeletal muscles in cerebral palsy and is used for anxiety.

mcq.question: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve reports anaphylaxis to penicillin. According to AHA 2021, which premedication is appropriate?
mcq.explanation: With penicillin anaphylaxis, cephalexin is avoided (cross-reactivity) and amoxicillin is contraindicated. Clindamycin was removed from the AHA 2021 guideline (C. difficile risk). Azithromycin 500 mg 30–60 min before is appropriate (doxycycline 100 mg is the other option).

mcq.question: Which antibiotic causes a reaction with alcohol and can produce a black hairy tongue?
mcq.explanation: Metronidazole (Flagyl): metallic taste, black hairy tongue, alcohol reaction. Azithromycin can cause a rare metallic taste but not an alcohol reaction.

mcq.question: Which statement about Periostat is correct?
options: A. It is a local minocycline microsphere placed in pockets ≥ 5 mm
B. It is a subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline taken 20 mg twice daily
C. It is a chlorhexidine chip with sustained release up to 10 days
D. It is bactericidal and kills periodontal pathogens directly
mcq.answer: B. It is a subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline taken 20 mg twice daily
mcq.explanation: Periostat = low-dose (subantimicrobial) doxycycline capsule, 20 mg BID, up to 9 months. Arestin is minocycline microspheres; PerioChip is chlorhexidine; tetracyclines are bacteriostatic.

mcq.question: A patient wants an adjunct after SRP for a single 6 mm site but is worried about staining. Which is the best choice?
mcq.explanation: PerioChip (2.5 mg chlorhexidine chip) is placed into a ≥ 5 mm pocket for localized periodontitis and causes no staining or taste alteration. CHX rinse stains teeth and tongue; systemic drugs are not site-specific.
